newsitem.title: INDIA: Congress party criticises India budget tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: Congress party criticises India budget tax cuts.

text.p: India's Congress party, which offers crucial support to Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's coalition, on Thursday criticised the government's new budget, saying some proposed tax cuts were not justified.

Congress officials, speaking to reporters after former finance minister Manmohan Singh addressed the party's deputies on the implications of the budget, said the party was also unhappy with an economic amnesty scheme to unearth black money.
"The government's voluntary disclosure scheme also came in for criticism," said Prithviraj Chavan, secretary of the Congress Parliamentary Party (CPP).
The Congress party offers make-or-break support to Deve Gowda's minority coalition that assumed power last June.
Congress spokesman Vithal Gadgil said the party had not taken a final stand on the budget, which was handed down last week.
"But we will ask the government to change some of the proposals," he said. He did not give details.
Asked if Congress would oppose the budget vote, which Deve Gowda needs to win to survive, Gadgil said: "We'll see that later. We are still discussing the issues."
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram said in his budget speech on February 28 that people having unaccounted money would not be penalised if they disclosed their wealth at a nominal tax of 30 percent.
"We felt that the tax on black money should at least be 40 percent. It was felt that 30 percent tax was too low," Chavan said.
Singh criticised Chidambaram's tax proposal for 1997/98 (April-March) in which corporate tax was reduced from 40 percent to 35 percent.
"Even the industry had not asked for it," Chauhan quoted Singh as telling the CPP meeting. There would be further discussions by the CPP on the budget on Tuesday, he said.
Chidambaram slashed the upper limit of personal income tax from 40 percent to 30 percent. Singh said that was not necessary as it only helped the rich.
Congress was also opposed to a Minimum Alternate Tax Chidambaram slapped on the industry in July last year, Chauhan said.
The tax applies to firms that earlier avoided taxation by ploughing back their profits using a legal loophole.
